info: Kōtukutuku is the world’s largest fuchsia. Its nectar-rich flowers attract tūī, bellbirds, and silvereyes, while the purple berries (kōnini) are edible for birds and people. Plant in moist, sheltered areas with good drainage and partial shade, protected when young. Avoid dry, exposed sites.

Tarata is a fragrant, fast-growing small tree which thrives in well-drained soils and full sun to partial shade. Plant tarata in mixed native hedges or shelterbelts with kōhūhū, koromiko and mānuka for structure and diversity. Its flowers attract pollinators, and it provides shelter for smaller forest understorey plants.

Whauwhi is a hardy, fast-growing small tree with glossy, divided leaves. It provides essential winter food for native birds such as kererū and tūī. It grows well on slopes and in mixed plantings with māhoe, horoeka and kōhūhū. Plant in well-drained soils and full to partial sun. Excellent for reforestation and bird gardens.

Tawhai raunui forms dense, dark forest canopies on dry ridges and mountain slopes. It prefers free-draining, slightly acidic soils and full sun. Beech litter enriches the soil with fungi that benefit other native trees.
Fast growing. The hardiest of the beeches and will grow in most areas, but not in frost hollows. Can grow 1m per year.
Slow growing forest tree with distinct juvenile leaves. Only plant under cover of taller plants. It produces blue fruit that birds love.

Houhere is a graceful small tree with white, starry flowers that bloom in summer. Prefers moist, fertile soils in sheltered positions. Its flowers attract insects, and it provides shade for understorey plants. Its bark can be used to make teas.

Long-leaved lacebark is a smaller, hardier relative of houhere. It has narrow leaves and produces clusters of white flowers in summer. It thrives in well-drained soils and full sun to partial shade. Ideal for rock gardens and mixed native borders.

Kapuka is a fast-growing, hardy tree with glossy leaves and small yellow flowers. It thrives in well-drained soils and full sun to partial shade. Its berries attract birds, and it provides shelter for smaller plants. Ideal for hedges and windbreaks.

Kahikatea is New Zealand’s tallest native tree, forming ancient swamp forests. It thrives in wet soils and floodplains. Plant in damp ground or near waterways with harakeke, tī kōuka, putaputawētā and cabbage trees for a natural wetland assemblage. Its fruit feeds kererū and other birds.
Māhoe is a fast-growing understorey tree with pale bark and violet berries for birds. They will generally grow up to 10m high.
Koromiko is a hardy, sun-loving shrub found in coastal and lowland regions. It bears spikes of white to lilac flowers that attract bees and butterflies. It tolerates wind and poor soils well.
Mountain tōtara is a compact, hardy conifer adapted to alpine and rocky conditions. It tolerates wind and frost, making it ideal for exposed gardens. Birds feed on its small red fruit.

Kōwhai produces bright yellow spring flowers rich in nectar for tūī and bellbirds. It prefers sunny, well-drained slopes. Avoid waterlogged soils. Seeds are toxic if ingested. The nectar is also toxic to bees.

Tawhai forms dense forest canopies at higher elevations. It prefers cool, moist, well-drained soils and partial shade. Tāhuna originally would have had silver beech dominating the upper, wetter valleys.

Mountain wineberry is a hardy shrub with red stems and small edible berries that attract birds. It thrives in moist, cool conditions and tolerates frost. Smaller than the Aristotelia serrata (wineberry), it is ideal for alpine and montane forests.
Fast growing small tree but does not like hard frosts. Good in sheltered gullies, hill slopes or near lakes

Matai is a slow-growing conifer with dark green foliage and red berries that attract birds. A slow growing, long lived podocarp. Hardy but prefers to grow under the shelter of other plants. Juvenile foliage wiry.

Putaputawētā is a small, spreading tree with marbled leaves and white flowers. It prefers moist soils and dappled light. It grows naturally with māhoe, kōtukutuku, and kahikatea. The larvae of native puriri moths inhabit its trunks.

Southern rātā is a striking forest tree with vivid red flowers that bloom in summer. It prefers cool, moist conditions and well-drained soils. Plant with tawhai, kānuka and māhoe in montane settings. Southern rātā is threatened in the wild due to possum browsing. It only flowers once every few years.

The Fierce Lancewood has distinctive spiny juvenile leaves that deter browsing animals. It prefers free-draining soils and sun or light shade. There are three species of lancewood, all called Horoeka by Māori. The rarest is fierce lancewood.
Orihou is a small, bushy tree with divided leaves and clusters of white flowers. It thrives in cool, moist forest conditions.

Tī Kōuka is a hardy, iconic tree with tall stems and sword-like leaves. It produces clusters of fragrant white flowers followed by dark berries that feed birds. Plant tī kōuka in sunny, well-drained or damp ground; it adapts to both wetlands and slopes. It is often the backbone of forest-edge ecosystems. Avoid heavy clay or full shade.

Inaka is a compact flax native to alpine slopes. It forms dense fans of green-red leaves and tall flower spikes rich in nectar. It thrives in full sun and well-drained soils, often alongside mountain tōtara and kānuka. Ideal for rock gardens and high-country restoration.

Karamū is a resilient shrub producing bright orange-red berries that attract birds. It prefers moist soils and full sun to light shade. Often planted with māhoe, tī kōuka, and harakeke for shelter and wildlife corridors. Great for stabilising banks and creating native hedges.

Mānuka is a hardy pioneer shrub with small aromatic leaves and nectar-rich flowers. It thrives in poor soils and full sun. Plant with kānuka, kōwhai and koromiko to encourage pollinators and soil recovery. Jewelled geckos have been reported in mānuka shrubland around Tāhuna.

Kānuka is a fast-growing tree that helps prepare soil for later forest species. It thrives in sunny, dry slopes. Its blossoms attract bees, and it provides shelter for seedlings of beech and podocarp trees.

Korokia is a common around lake whakatipu, forming tight bushes with small yellow flowers in spring followed by orange to red fruit. Slow growing but very hardy. It tolerates wind, salt, and poor soils.

Kōhūhū is a small native tree that can grow up to 10 metres tall in the wild. One of the most common small trees throughout the district forming a many-stemmed bright green tree. Can be used for hedges as bushy and readily trimmed. It has fragrant yellow flowers that bloom in spring which are followed by woody seed capsules that split open to reveal bright orange seeds that is readily spread by birds.

A robust fern found in montane and alpine forests forming large clumps up to 1m tall, but generally smaller. It thrives in cool, moist, shaded environments. Ideal for rock gardens and shaded borders, it pairs well with other ferns and shade-loving plants.
An attractive spreading alpine plant with white daisy-like flowers on short stalks. Prefers open, well-drained ground and full sun. Suitable for rock gardens and dry slopes.
A smaller Astelia species with silver-grey leaves. Prefers damp, cool conditions but not full wetland. Excellent for shaded, moist slopes or under light canopy.

A hardy grass that grows on both damp and drier sites. Toi Toi alongside native sedges, flax, and tussock can surround wetlands and ponds, and provide the perfect playground for pūkeko and pūtakitaki (paradise ducks).
A robust tussock suited for dry, exposed areas. Its golden-brown seed heads create soft texture in native landscapes. Prefers well-drained soils.
A reddish tussock that thrives in moist sites but tolerates dryness. Provides excellent cover and movement in the landscape. Key species in tussock grasslands.
A fine native grass forming small tufts with drooping flower heads. Attractive but uncommon and seldom available in nurseries. Prefers dry, open habitats.
A smaller, stiffer form of silver tussock. Very hardy and tolerant of poor soils and wind exposure. Excellent for alpine or dry garden plantings.
A tufted bluish native grass found in forests. Prefers shade and moisture. Uncommon in nurseries but ideal for forest restoration or shaded native gardens.
A small native tussock with bluish leaves. Very hardy, growing on rocks and stony ground. Excellent for alpine plantings and dry slopes.
Common in large plantings, forming silvery grass clumps. Looks best on lean, drier soils where its form stays tight and upright. Can become untidy in rich soil.
A large, tussock-forming sedge of swamps and wetlands. Excellent for stabilising banks and creating native wetland habitat. Provides shelter for wetland fauna.
A smaller flax species with soft, drooping leaves. Grows in most soils except frost hollows. Excellent for mixed native borders and damp slopes.
A robust flax species found around water and wetlands, but also tolerating dry sites. Provides nectar for birds and material for weaving. Forms the backbone of wetland restoration plantings.
A large flax-like plant with drooping leaves, preferring partial shade and damp forest conditions. Adds lush texture to shaded native gardens.

Snow Tōtara thrives on rocky slopes, alpine and montane sites with good drainage, and can tolerate frost and snow. Its berries attract native birds, and it is ideal for low forest cover. Plant alongside inaka, mountain tōtara, harakeke, and kānuka to mimic natural alpine vegetation.

Mingimingi is a dense, bushy shrub with small leaves and berries that attract birds. It thrives in moist soils and full sun to light shade. Dense wide-angled branches superb to use as hedge hidout for insects and lizards
Mikimiki is the tallest coprosma with narrow, brownish leaves. Prefers shelter and is happy growing under other trees.
Fast growing, deciduous tree that eventually forms a roundheaded tree. Very hardy but slow if too dry.
